newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: Bishop Belo sees no quick solution to E.Timor.
newsitem.headline: Bishop Belo sees no quick solution to E.Timor.

text.p: East Timor's Nobel peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo said on Thursday he saw no quick solution to the problems of the troubled territory despite international interest in its future.

He said a fresh initiative by U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan and a visit to East Timor by a U.S. government human rights expert were unlikely to solve the problems of the former Portuguese colony annexed by Indonesia two decades ago.
"(For many years), I hear the same things, the same resolutions," Belo told Reuters in an interview at his home in Dili, capital of Roman Catholic-dominated East Timor.
"I am not hopeful," said the bishop, an apostolic administrator who reports directly to Rome.
Indonesia invaded East Timor in December 1975 with tacit Western support after civil war broke out there following the departure of Portuguese colonial authorities.
Indonesia incorporated East Timor as its 27th province the following July in a move not recognised by the United Nations.
John Shattuck, U.S. assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, arrived in Dili on Thursday on a fact-finding visit.

At the same time, the newly-appointed U.N. special envoy for East Timor, Jamsheed Marker, arrived in Jakarta on what the United Nations described as a familiarisation visit. He will visit East Timor over the weekend.
U.S. officials said the timing of the visits was coincidental and that Shattuck had previously postponed a trip scheduled for last year.

"The purpose of this visit is to emphasise the importance the United States places on positive discussions under the auspices of the U.N. secretary-general on the issue of East Timor," Shattuck told reporters at Dili airport.
"It emphasises the great importance of the issue of East Timor and human rights, generally speaking. I Look forward to... find out more about the situation," he said.

Shattuck met the territory's governor, Abilio Soares, and the local commander of the Indonesian military on Thursday. He was also due to meet Belo and have talks with local human rights activists before leaving on Friday for Cambodia.

Marker, a former Pakistani ambassador to the United Nations appointed by Annan last month as his special assistant for East Timor, met President Suharto and Foreign Minister Ali Alatas after his arrival in Jakarta on Thursday.
He told reporters after meeting Suharto that a productive dialogue was needed to achieve an acceptable international solution over East Timor.
He visited Portugal earlier this month and said in Lisbon he hoped to speed up so-far unproductive U.N.-sponsored talks between Portugal and Indonesia over East Timor's future.
Belo, who spoke cheerfully and smiled frequently during his interview, said little had changed in East Timor for years.
"For me, it is the same, there is no substantial change," he said. "There are demonstrations by the young people, they arrest them and put them in detention without trial."
"This is our daily cross. Here we have (experienced) fear many times, given the number of soldiers, the number of troops."
The bishop, who was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace prize with self-exiled independence activist Jose Ramos Horta, said some autonomy from Jakarta was essential for any solution.
"Timor is different culturally, historically, from other parts of Indonesia," he said. "Give some concessions, let the people have their autonomy."
